faq.a: Take a detailed occupational history and order a chest X‑ray or bedside ultrasound if radiography is unavailable.
faq.q: What is the first step when a worker presents with chronic cough?

faq.a: Occupational asthma improves when the patient avoids the workplace trigger; perform serial peak flow monitoring at work and away.
faq.q: How do you differentiate occupational asthma from allergic asthma?

faq.a: When blood lead exceeds 80 µg/dL or the patient has symptomatic encephalopathy, renal impairment, or severe anemia.
faq.q: When is chelation indicated for lead exposure?

exam: What key questions in the occupational history would you ask a miner with dyspnoea? — Identify duration of exposure, type of dust, use of respirators, latency period, and smoking status.

A factory worker presents with peripheral neuropathy and anemia; blood lead is unavailable. How do you proceed? — Look for basophilic stippling, gastrointestinal colic, and consider empirical chelation if severe, while arranging referral for testing.

How does silicosis differ radiologically from sarcoidosis? — Silicosis shows upper‑lobe nodular opacities with eggshell calcified lymph nodes; sarcoidosis often has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules.

Which occupational exposure is most strongly linked to bladder cancer in East Africa? — Aromatic amines such as those in dye and rubber industries; advise regular urine cytology if exposure is prolonged.

A nurse had a needle stick from an HIV‑positive patient. What immediate steps are required? — Wash site, start post‑exposure prophylaxis within 72 h, test baseline HIV, and arrange follow‑up serology.
What are the red‑flag signs of acute pesticide poisoning? — Seizures, respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils, and altered mental status; treat with atropine and supportive ventilation.
Why is routine chest X‑ray insufficient for early asbestos disease? — Early pleural plaques and interstitial changes may be invisible; high‑resolution CT is needed for detection.

How would you counsel a small‑scale farmer using organophosphate insecticides about prevention? — Use gloves and masks, avoid skin contact, store chemicals securely, and rotate to less toxic alternatives.

ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Occupational health examines work‑related hazards, their clinical impact and prevention. In East African hospitals clinicians must recognise common toxic, infectious and ergonomic exposures even when diagnostic tools are limited.

b: Ask about job title, tasks, duration, protective equipment, and recent changes.
Identify latency periods (e.g., asbestos‑related disease may appear decades later).
sections.p: Occupational health is the discipline that identifies, evaluates and controls workplace hazards that cause disease or injury. Diagnosis relies on a focused occupational history and linking clinical findings to known exposures.

b: Mild: exposure documented, no clinical signs.
Moderate: early symptoms, reversible changes.
Severe: organ damage, irreversible disease.
sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement and functional loss rather than a universal stage system. For example, silicosis is staged as simple (asymptomatic) or progressive massive fibrosis (dyspnoea, radiographic nodules).

b: Chemical: vinyl chloride (PVC factories), arsenic (metal smelting), nickel, chromium, pesticides.
Biological: TB exposure in health‑care workers, hepatitis B from needle sticks.
Physical: noise‑induced hearing loss, heat stress, vibration.
Ergonomic: heavy lifting, repetitive strain, poor posture.
sections.p: Causes are grouped into chemical, physical, biological and ergonomic hazards. In East Africa the most frequent are:

b: Respiratory: chronic cough, dyspnoea, wheeze (silicosis, asbestos, dust).
Dermatologic: contact dermatitis, hyperpigmentation (arsenic, nickel).
Neurologic: peripheral neuropathy (lead, organic solvents).
Systemic: fatigue, weight loss, anemia (chronic chemical exposure).
sections.p: Presentation varies with the agent. Common patterns include:

t.b: Detects pneumoconiosis, pleural plaques, or TB; if unavailable, use bedside ultrasound for pleural effusion.
Assesses obstructive vs restrictive pattern; if not available, use peak flow and clinical assessment.
Confirms lead poisoning; if lab unavailable, look for basophilic stippling and neuro‑cognitive signs.
Screen for hepatotoxic chemicals (vinyl chloride, arsenic); if normal, repeat after exposure cessation.
Identifies specific agents and duration; guides targeted testing.

b: Progressive massive fibrosis → respiratory failure.
Heavy metal poisoning → renal failure, encephalopathy.
Carcinogen exposure → lung, bladder, skin cancers.
Severe noise exposure → sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
sections.p: Complications may be irreversible and life‑threatening.

b: Immediate cessation or reduction of exposure; provide appropriate PPE.
Chelation (e.g., dimercaprol) for acute lead poisoning; avoid if renal failure present.
Bronchodilators for obstructive symptoms; steroids only for acute inflammation.
Vaccinate health‑care workers against hepatitis B; provide post‑exposure prophylaxis for needle sticks.
Referral to occupational‑health specialist for long‑term monitoring.
sections.p: Management combines removal from exposure, specific therapy and supportive care.

b: Annual clinical review with spirometry for dust‑exposed workers.
Biannual blood lead or mercury levels in high‑risk industries.
Enforce local safety regulations (Kenyan Occupational Safety and Health Act).
Education on safe handling of chemicals and use of PPE.
Occupational asthma improves when exposure stops; allergic asthma persists despite avoidance.
Silicosis shows upper‑lobe nodules and a history of silica dust; sarcoidosis may have bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
sections.p: Occupational asthma vs. allergic asthma; silicosis vs. sarcoidosis; lead neuropathy vs. diabetic neuropathy.

b: Chest X‑ray can be normal in early silicosis; high‑resolution CT is more sensitive.
Blood lead may be normal after recent chelation; repeat after 2‑4 weeks.
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal early in disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute respiratory distress after chemical inhalation
Sudden loss of hearing or vision following exposure
Severe abdominal pain with suspected heavy‑metal poisoning
